deep.reconstruction:
Heading: 'Classificatio divisorum formarum □+α, α designante numerum primum aut numeri primi duplum', dated June 1797, labelled Tab. A.1. It classifies the divisors of x^2+α, that is, the binary quadratic forms of determinant −α. On this page α = p runs through the primes 1993, 1913, 1889, 1873, 1801, 1777, 1753 and 1721. All of them are ≡ 1 mod 8; the next page continues downward with 1697, …, 1361.

The number after each prime is the class number h of properly primitive positive forms (a,b,c) = ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 with b^2−ac = −p, i.e. h(−4p) in modern terms:
• h(1993)=24, h(1913)=36, h(1889)=72, h(1873)=12, h(1801)=28, h(1777)=24, h(1753)=20, h(1721)=52.

The tables. In every case the class group is cyclic. Gauss chooses a generator g, apparently the class with the smallest prime a that generates:
• (11,3,182) for 1993; (3,1,638) for 1913; (7,1,270) for 1889; (23,6,83) for 1873;
• (11,5,166) for 1801; (11,4,163) for 1777; (7,2,251) for 1753; (3,1,574) for 1721.

Row k lists the class g^k by its first coefficient a with the middle coefficient b in parentheses. The third coefficient is implicit: c = (b^2+p)/a. In the 1993 and 1913 tables the row label 'k.h−k' records that g^(h−k) is the inverse class (a,−b,c). The last row k = h/2 is always the ambiguous class (2,1,(p+1)/2) of order 2. Sometimes b is omitted, and in 1721 the pair is written 'a.b'.

Example (my check) for 1993:
• g = (11,3,182).
• g^2: solve B ≡ 3 (mod 11) with B^2 ≡ −1993 (mod 121). This gives B = −8 and the form (121,−8,17) ~ (17,8,121), matching row 2: 17(8).
• Similarly (23,6,83)^2 ~ (26,5,73) for 1873, matching row 2.

Third column. Against the even rows (the squares, i.e. the principal genus) Gauss writes representations p = x^2+y^2+z^2, e.g. 1993 = 43^2+12^2+0^2 = 33^2+30^2+2^2 = …. The placement follows the classical correspondence (my verification). For a primitive v = (x,y,z) with |v|^2 = p, the orthogonal complement of v in Z^3 is a binary lattice of determinant p, and its Gram form lies in the class written in that row. Examples:
• (43,12,0) gives (1,0,1993), the principal class.
• (33,30,2): the complement basis (2,0,−33), (0,1,−15) gives (1093,495,226) ~ (17,8,121) = row 2.
• (29,24,24) gives (2,−29,1417) ~ (2,1,997) = row 12.

Where the list is complete it agrees with r3(p) = 12·h(−4p), counting 24 signed orderings for types (x,y,0) and (x,y,y) and 48 otherwise:
• 1993: 24 + 5·48 + 24 = 288 = 12·24.
• 1889: 24 + 17·48 + 24 = 864 = 12·72.
• 1873: 24 + 2·48 + 24 = 144 = 12·12.
• 1801: 24 + 6·48 + 24 = 336 = 12·28.

The lists for 1913, 1777, 1753 and 1721 are left incomplete. For 1721 only representations with x = 36 were tried.

Bottom line: '8 | 72.52.36.28.24.24.20.12 | 268 . 33½' gives the 8 class numbers sorted, their sum 268, and their mean 33.5. This is an empirical study of the average class number (cf. Disq. Arith. art. 302); the next page gives 10 primes with sum 372 and mean 37.2.

The rotated marginal numbers are unrelated scratch work, not interpretable.
errors: 1801, row 0: written '25.34.0' but 25^2+34^2 = 1781. The correct value is 35^2+24^2+0^2 = 1801, so the digits are transposed (a slip or a misreading).
1913, row 18: transcribed '39.4.14' gives 1733. The correct entry is 39.14.14 (1521+196+196 = 1913), which as a type (x,y,y) also fits the ambiguous class (2,1,957).

1889, row 26: '40 (1)' is impossible since 40 does not divide 1+1889. Composition (g^27·g^−1 with g^27 = (27,−1,70)) gives (10,1,189), so it should read 10(1). The digit may be overwritten in the manuscript.
1889, row 9: '36(34)' is impossible since 34^2+1889 = 3045 is not divisible by 36. The image reads 35(34): 3045/35 = 87.
1873, row 2: the struck-out entry should be 42.10.3 (1764+100+9 = 1873), which is needed to make r3 = 144. If Gauss wrote 41.10.3 (= 1790), it was a slip he cancelled.
Third-column lists for 1913 (rows 2, 10, 12, 16), 1777 (rows 6, 8, 12), 1753 and 1721 are incomplete. These are omissions, not errors.
In the 1801 table some b are not reduced, e.g. 25(18) and 34(33). These are still correct forms.

results.what: Tables of the (cyclic) class groups of positive forms of determinant −p for primes p ≡ 1 mod 8 near 1700–2000, listing every class as a power of a generator (a,b,c)
results.modern_name: class group Cl(−4p) and its structure; tables of class numbers and class groups
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, arts. 305–306; posthumous class-number tables in Werke II)

results.what: Matching representations p = x^2+y^2+z^2 with classes of the principal genus (orthogonal-complement form), consistent with r3(p) = 12h(−4p)
results.modern_name: Gauss's three-squares theorem and the class-number formula for r3(n)

results.what: Empirical mean of class numbers h(−4p) over a block of primes (sum 268, mean 33.5)
results.modern_name: average order of class numbers (Gauss's conjecture, Disq. Arith. art. 302; proved by Lipschitz/Mertens/Siegel)

deep.surprise_reason: These are 1797 working tables behind well-known Disquisitiones material: class groups, the genus/three-squares correspondence and average class numbers. It is a nice dated record of how Gauss explicitly placed three-square representations into classes, but nothing here goes beyond what is credited to him.

checkable.asserts: third-column entries for 1993 are representations as sums of three squares
all listed forms (a,b,(b^2+p)/a) for 1993 have determinant −1993

checkable.asserts: class numbers stated in the headers

checkable.sympy: len([(x,y,z) for x in range(-45,46) for y in range(-45,46) for z in range(-45,46) if x*x+y*y+z*z==1993]) == 12*24

checkable.asserts: 1889 row 26 must be 10(1), not 40(1); row 9 is 35(34)

transcription_corrections: 1889 row 26: '40 (1)' should be 10(1), mathematically forced; possibly a Gauss slip or an overwritten digit.
1873 row 2 struck entry: '41.10.3' is probably '42.10.3', the correct value.
1801 row 0: '25.34.0' is as written but should be 35.24.0, mathematically forced.
1721 rows use 'a.b' for 'a(b)'; the stray '9.4' / '27.13' etc. are correct as forms (9,4,193), (27,13,70).
